title: Parse an Integer
statement:
Turn a string of digits into an `int`, by hand.

## Your function

```
int parse_int(const char *s, int *out);
```

If the whole string is a valid decimal integer, store its value through `out`
and return `1`. Otherwise return `0` and leave `*out` alone.

Valid means: an optional `+` or `-`, then one or more digits, then the end of
the string. No spaces, and nothing after the digits. Every value used in the
tests fits in an `int`.

## Watch out

- `""`, `"-"` and `"+"` are not valid: a sign on its own is not a number.
- `"12a"` is not valid either. Stopping at the first bad character and
  returning what you had is what `atoi` does, and is not what is wanted here.
- Leading zeros are fine: `"007"` is 7.
- `c - '0'` converts a digit character to its value. The digits are guaranteed
  to be consecutive in any C character set, which is why this works and the
  same trick on letters does not.
- Return `0` *before* touching `*out`, so a caller who ignored the return
  value at least keeps whatever was in the variable.

tests.name: a lone sign
tests.description: A sign has to be followed by at least one digit.

tests.name: trailing rubbish
tests.description: The whole string has to be a number, so this is a rejection rather than a 12.
